claims.text: Adding approximately 2–5 at.% zirconium to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy improves its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 2–5 at.% zirconium improves the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
The zirconium-free baseline has limited glass-forming ability and lower thermal stability.
Zirconium addition enhances atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Zirconium and phosphorus have a strong negative heat of mixing.
Enhanced atomic-size mismatch and negative zirconium–phosphorus mixing enthalpy increase atomic packing frustration.
The size and bonding characteristics of zirconium introduce local structural distortions.
Zirconium-induced local distortions inhibit crystal nucleation and growth.
Inhibition of crystal nucleation and growth raises the kinetic barrier to crystallization.
A higher kinetic barrier to crystallization enhances amorphous-phase formation and thermal stability.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a higher critical casting thickness than the zirconium-free baseline.
The zirconium-modified alloy will have a higher onset crystallization temperature than the zirconium-free baseline.
The benefit should occur under moderate cooling conditions where atomic-scale rearrangements govern amorphous-structure formation.
Zirconium contents substantially outside 2–5 at.% may fail to provide the predicted improvements.
Extremely high cooling rates may make the zirconium intervention ineffective.
Excessive destabilizing elements may negate the zirconium-induced improvement.
Zirconium has demonstrated beneficial effects in similar glass-forming systems.
